newsitem.title: USA: Futures heads stress user needs in product choice.
newsitem.headline: Futures heads stress user needs in product choice.

text.p: Contracts launched by U.S. futures exchanges should better reflect customers' needs and interests to avoid wasting effort at a time when firms' profit margins are shrinking, futures executives said on Thursday.

Larry Mollner, executive vice president of Dean Witter Reynolds, questioned the need for products such as butter and catastrophic insurance futures during a panel at the Futures Industry Association annual conference here.
He said he was "not sure" futures commission merchants or their customers cared enough about such products to justify investing the money and time educating brokers about them.
The Chicago Mercantile Exchange in early September revived its butter futures contract. The Chicago Board of Trade offers a group of catastrophic insurance futures and options.
Meeting customer requirements for contracts is paramount, said Hal Hansen, president of Cargill Investor Services.

"If our customers aren't interested, then we have very little interest in going out and pushing water uphill," Hansen said, adding that unless there is strong customer demand for a product, "then we don't even get involved."
Chicago Board of Trade Chairman Patrick Arbor said he thinks the CBOT continues to develop viable products that FCMs want, such as the CBOT's new yield curve spread futures.

But he also predicted that futures exchanges increasingly will investigate non-standardized listings that emulate over-the-counter products, which the exchanges have complained are eating into their business.

"I do believe you're going to see the exchanges coming out with a bevy of products that look very much like over-the-counter" products, Arbor added. -Derivatives Desk(312)408-8750/E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com
